channel.title: Sandboxing - what are the best options?
channel.description:
Hi!
Having used other Debian based distros for many years, I am finally moving to Kicksecure (running in Qubes OS VM’s).
However, one thing that confuse me is sandboxing. I have been using Firejail up until now, but now considering to use something else due to the SUID issue.
For Firefox, Flatpak sandboxing break Firefox’s internal sandbox. Is there really no decent way of sandboxing browsers in Linux? The only thing that seems to increase security (without SUID issues or breaking Firefox internal sandboxing) seems to be writing an Apparmor profile, does that make sense?
For Evince and Libreoffice the choice seems to be between Flatpak sandboxing or MAC with Apparmor (AFAIK doing both is not an option). What would be the most secure option?
For other applications like GIMP and the file manager, Flatpak seems to be the only realistic option as they do not have Apparmor profiles.
I am trying to avoid malware/attackers getting access to certain files in my home folder, or becoming root. I know that no sandboxing can compare with VM isolation, but for me it’s important to prevent that the VMs do no keep getting infected as well. And running every suspicions file and webpage in a new VM would disrupt my workflow too much.

item.title: Sandboxing - what are the best options?
item.dc:creator: arraybolt3
item.description:
ks44:

The only thing that seems to increase security (without SUID issues or breaking Firefox internal sandboxing) seems to be writing an Apparmor profile, does that make sense?

AppArmor under Debian Trixie is of very limited use. UNIX socket mediation and D-Bus mediation does not work (contrary to what the manpage claims), so if a process is permitted to open any single UNIX socket, it can open all UNIX sockets on the system that file permissions allow it to reach. This includes the D-Bus socket, which (among other things) allows a process to escape AppArmor confinement by loading a malicious LD_PRELOAD variable into a systemd user manager.

ks44:

For Evince and Libreoffice the choice seems to be between Flatpak sandboxing or MAC with Apparmor (AFAIK doing both is not an option). What would be the most secure option?

Difficult to say. AppArmor is frequently not very useful as covered above, but Flatpak has its own set of problems. See:

flatkill.org

Flatpak - a security nightmare

Flatpak - a security nightmare

(Note that Flatpak isn’t necessarily useless or harmful if used carefully by a sufficiently skilled user, the point made by the above site is mostly that it provides very little real-world protection when used casually in the way a usual user would.)

Kicksecure is working on our own application sandboxing framework in an attempt to address the limitations of existing solutions:

Separate (some) user applications from the operating system Development
Android, iOS, macOS, and Chrome OS all provide a level of separation between user-installed applications and the operating system. The operating system may provide certain applications to the user, but those applications are not installed by the user and generally cannot be uninstalled or replaced. User-controllable applications are separated from the rest of the system, and generally are sandboxed to prevent them from doing damage if they turn out to be malicious or become compromised. Debian …

The current plan is to use systemd-nspawn as a backend, and write a sophisticated wrapper around it that makes it user-friendly while discouraging unsafe uses. The system being build (sandbox-manager-dist) does not yet exist in any usable form, but systemd-nspawn is available from the Debian repositories. You may be able to use it to do what you want, though it will take some effort.
